# Apple Human Interface Guidelines

Use the relevant Apple guidance to make concrete design decisions. This package
contains a router, 13 family routes, 158 operational topic skills, and supporting
article-level references. It is
independent of Apple. The sources are a dated English HIG snapshot; check the
official source when a task depends on a newer release or a disputed detail.

## Route the task

1. Identify the target platform, device context, and user task from the request or
   project. Ask for the platform only when it materially affects the answer and
   cannot be inferred. Preserve the user's framework and product requirements.
2. Select the relevant family below and read that family's `SKILL.md`. Follow its
   link to the exact topic procedure under `.topics/` and read that `SKILL.md`.
   Apply its decision procedure, then consult its supporting article for facts
   and platform qualifications. Topic skills are explicitly read by installed
   file path; automatic nested discovery is not required.
   For platform support, product feasibility, or platform adaptation, first read each relevant
   platform's Getting started procedure, then the specific component or technology
   procedure. Check both the platform model and the surface's support limits.
3. Before finalizing the route, search the [complete topic index](references/topic-index.md)
   for the task's concepts as well as component or framework names. Its trigger
   descriptions connect everyday product requests to Apple's topic names; users
   need not name an Apple framework. Read the owning family and matching topic
   procedure before its supporting reference. Search relevant rows instead of
   loading the full corpus for a narrow question.
   For a screenshot-specific or animated example, also consult its
   [original visual explanation](references/media/index.md) when available.
4. Apply shared guidance and the target platform's documented differences. A
   missing platform subsection means no additional rule is stated; it does not
   prove support, nonapplicability, or identical behavior across platforms.
5. Compose families when the task crosses them: a component can also require
   accessibility, typography, localization, input, or system-experience guidance.
   Map the brief's material decisions to their owning topics. Read the owning
   procedure for each explicit concern, such as privacy or accessibility, as well
   as the affected components; a neighboring procedure's reminder is insufficient.
   Use [platform and task routes](references/platforms-and-tasks.md) when useful.
   In a review, map each supplied control to its candidate component procedure
   even when markup or behavior is missing. Use it to frame inspection questions;
   missing evidence neither proves a defect nor removes that control from scope.

All paths are relative to **this installed package**, not the shell's current
directory. No Python, network, sibling skill installation, or authoring cache is
required to read the guidance.

| Task | Read this topic skill |
|---|---|
| Platform conventions, design principles, games, device adaptation | [Getting started](subskills/apple-hig-getting-started/SKILL.md) |
| Accessibility, typography, color, materials, layout, localization, privacy | [Foundations](subskills/apple-hig-foundations/SKILL.md) |
| Onboarding, loading, search, sharing, accounts, feedback, media, settings | [Patterns](subskills/apple-hig-patterns/SKILL.md) |
| Charts, images, text views, embedded web content | [Content](subskills/apple-hig-content/SKILL.md) |
| Lists, collections, split views, tab views, disclosure and grouping | [Layout and organization](subskills/apple-hig-layout-and-organization/SKILL.md) |
| Buttons, menus, toolbars, menu bar, ornaments and actions | [Menus and actions](subskills/apple-hig-menus-and-actions/SKILL.md) |
| Sidebars, tab bars, search fields, tokens and path controls | [Navigation and search](subskills/apple-hig-navigation-and-search/SKILL.md) |
| Alerts, sheets, popovers, panels, scrolling and windows | [Presentation](subskills/apple-hig-presentation/SKILL.md) |
| Text fields, pickers, sliders, toggles, selection controls | [Selection and input](subskills/apple-hig-selection-and-input/SKILL.md) |
| Progress, activity, gauges and ratings | [Status](subskills/apple-hig-status/SKILL.md) |
| Widgets, Live Activities, notifications, Siri snippets and system surfaces | [System experiences](subskills/apple-hig-system-experiences/SKILL.md) |
| Touch, keyboard, pointer, focus, eyes, gestures, controllers and sensors | [Inputs](subskills/apple-hig-inputs/SKILL.md) |
| Apple Pay, purchases, Siri, VoiceOver, AI, CarPlay and integrations | [Technologies](subskills/apple-hig-technologies/SKILL.md) |

## Perform the requested work

Inspect the supplied brief, flow, code, specification or image before deciding
what is wrong or choosing a framework. Use the user's requested mode:

- **Design:** produce an implementable specification or interaction/state model
  from the topic's decision procedure, with concrete transitions and acceptance
  checks. Connect choices to the user's task and target platform.
- **Implement:** prefer the project's native system components when they supply
  the needed behavior. HIG explains experience requirements; verify API names,
  availability, and code against the appropriate SDK documentation. Make the
  authorized changes in the existing stack; a prose explanation alone does not
  complete an implementation request.
- **Review:** describe the observed problem, its effect, the relevant HIG rule,
  and a concrete correction. Separate source-backed findings from your own
  suggested improvements. Do not invent violations without inspecting evidence.
- **Adapt:** preserve the product task, data and useful state while applying the
  destination platform's interaction model. Patch the supplied artifact or give
  an explicit before/after contract when a design specification is requested.

Topic procedures are framework agnostic. Their worked examples and pseudocode
teach decisions, not a requirement to replace the project's technology. Load
related procedures only for a decision that actually depends on them.

Complete the topic's observable checks and report passed, failed and not executed
separately. Reading a file, citing Apple, or proposing a test does not establish
runtime behavior. Static code or screenshots cannot prove assistive-technology
order, native rendering, physical comfort, haptics, or SDK compilation.

Include official article/section links for material recommendations. Preserve
qualifications such as “consider,” “prefer,” and “avoid”; do not turn design
advice into invented universal requirements. Retain units and platform scope for
numerical specifications. If source passages conflict, describe the conflict
and the conservative application rather than silently changing the source.

## Source boundaries

This is comprehensive local guidance, not a verbatim Apple manual or an SDK API
reference. Original media explanations are supplementary to article references;
the source page remains useful for visual demonstrations. Source snapshots and
review status live in the repository's coverage report, outside ordinary skill
loading. Do not infer that a source has been independently reviewed just because
its local file exists.

Historical `navigation-bars` links now resolve to current Toolbars guidance;
`in-app-purchase` resolves to Apple In-App Purchase. The old Touch Bar and Messages
for Business HIG pages were unavailable at this snapshot. Do not fabricate their
current rules. Translations, archived pages, and complete linked SDK/WWDC libraries
are outside the source boundary.

# Apple HIG: Platform and task adaptation

Use this family to select and compose topic procedures. Infer the platform and
requested work from the supplied project; preserve its framework and constraints.

## Work through the decision

1. Identify the person’s primary task and the target platform before translating a screen. Read that platform’s procedure; use Principles to resolve hierarchy and Designing for games only for gameplay.
2. Compare navigation, window/scene model, primary input, attention duration and state restoration. Preserve the product task while changing the interaction appropriate to the destination platform.
3. For device changes such as opening an iPhone Duo or resizing an iPad window, specify what selection, editing state and route survive each transition.
4. Deliver a platform-decision matrix or an adaptation patch, with concrete acceptance scenarios for each materially different interaction.

## Enter the topic procedure

inspect actual evidence and return findings; for an implementation request, make

name: apple-hig-designing-for-ios
description: Use when creating, reviewing, or adapting an iPhone experience for handheld touch, interrupted use, orientation changes, and system entrypoints.
---

# Make the iPhone task usable in the hand

Read [Designing for iOS](../../references/designing-for-ios.md). Inspect the current task, its entry and return points, supported orientations, input, and any supplied implementation. Distinguish a brief check from extended work. For a review, anchor problems to supplied screens/behavior; for design or adaptation, revise the requested artifact in its existing stack.

Choose what must remain immediately visible during the task. A brief check needs its result and primary action close together; extended editing can expose additional controls without crowding the initial screen. Put frequent touch actions within comfortable reach, generally toward the middle/lower display, while preserving system navigation and swipe-back behavior. Move secondary commands into a short discoverable path rather than shrinking every control to fit.

Trace interruption and resumption: preserve the selected item, draft, or playback context when another app takes focus. Specify portrait/landscape and enlarged-text rearrangements without inventing a new navigation hierarchy for each orientation. Use touch and onscreen keyboard as the baseline, then offer appropriate voice or accessory paths. Add location, biometric, payment, or motion features only when their benefit reduces task effort and access is appropriate.

For repeated out-of-app actions, choose a relevant system entrypoint and a precise destination: a quick action starts an action, search opens the found content, and a widget exposes a useful glance. Do not add every entrypoint to every app.

**Before → decision → after:** A parcel app opens a dense desktop-style table and requires opening three menus to find the latest delivery. A handheld glance needs delivery state first. The revised home screen shows the active parcel and “Show pickup code,” keeps history one step away, and returns a widget tap to that parcel rather than a generic home screen.

Deliver a revised screen/flow or implementation plus interruption, orientation, and text-size acceptance checks. Fail if the primary action becomes unreachable, Back conflicts with a custom gesture, or resuming loses work. Screenshot review cannot establish touch comfort or actual system integration; state pending device checks.

For detailed adaptation use [Layout](../../../apple-hig-foundations/.topics/apple-hig-layout/SKILL.md); for custom touch gestures use [Gestures](../../../apple-hig-inputs/.topics/apple-hig-gestures/SKILL.md); for a chosen glance use [Widgets](../../../apple-hig-system-experiences/.topics/apple-hig-widgets/SKILL.md).

# Designing for iOS Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-ios) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. An iPhone experience must work both during brief checks on the move and through extended games, browsing, or media sessions. People switch among apps frequently. ## Best practices - Design for a medium-sized, dense display viewed at roughly 1–2 feet, usually held in one or both hands. Accommodate portrait and landscape use. - Keep primary content and actions clear, with secondary operations reachable through a small number of interactions rather than many simultaneous controls. - Support touch gestures, onscreen keyboards, and voice; use motion sensors, nearby spatial interactions, or personal information only where they improve the task. - Put frequent touch controls within comfortable reach, commonly the middle or lower display. Preserve swipe-back navigation and list-row gestures. - Adapt to orientation, Dark Mode, and Dynamic Type without breaking context. - With permission, use platform data and services to reduce typing: location, biometric authentication, and payments are examples. - Integrate appropriate system entry points: widgets, Home Screen quick actions, Spotlight search, Shortcuts, and activity views. Their familiar behavior helps people act outside the main app. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-ios) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here.

# Apple HIG: Map user actions to input and alternatives

Use this family to select and compose topic procedures. Infer the platform and
requested work from the supplied project; preserve its framework and constraints.

## Work through the decision

1. Identify the action and available hardware/input context, then enter the keyboard, pointer, focus, eyes, gestures, controller, Pencil, Crown or sensor procedure.
2. Preserve reserved system gestures and familiar input meanings. Separate targeting, focus, selection and activation; define feedback and reachable alternatives for the actions people must complete.
3. Account for comfort, precision, fatigue and switching between available inputs. Custom inputs should not remove an accessible route to an essential action.
4. Deliver an action-to-input mapping, focus/selection states and observable verification scenarios. Keep code/static observations separate from physical comfort, eye/hand and hardware checks.

name: apple-hig-camera-control
description: Use when designing or reviewing iPhone Camera Control overlay functions, slider or picker choices, capture-mode availability, or locked capture entry.
---

# Make hardware adjustments predictable during capture

Read [Camera Control](../../references/camera-control.md). Inspect capture modes, existing controls, value models, viewfinder layout, and supported devices. The source describes iPhone 16/16 Pro and excludes other platforms; verify current hardware/API availability when implementing beyond that snapshot. Choose design, review, or adaptation mode and retain the existing capture stack.

Inventory the fixed control set. Use sliders for ranges and pickers for discrete choices; enable/disable controls by capture mode rather than dynamically adding/removing them. Put common functions near the middle and rare ones at the ends, accounting for the system remembering the last-used control.

Give each function a short name and an available SF Symbol representing function rather than live state; custom symbols are unsupported here. Expose meaningful units/localized values and useful prominent range values so sliding can settle precisely. Reserve overlay/label space beside the hardware control in portrait and landscape, allowing Dynamic Type enlargement. Hide duplicate app controls while the overlay is present without hiding unrelated needed information. Consider the locked camera capture extension for relevant system entrypoints.

**Before → decision → after:** A camera app adds/removes white-balance choices whenever modes change and uses a custom icon whose shape varies with temperature. Decision: the hardware overlay needs a stable function set and function identity. After, white balance remains in its fixed position but is disabled in unsupported modes, uses an available function symbol, and displays a localized temperature value while duplicate onscreen controls recede during adjustment.

Deliver the fixed function inventory, slider/picker/value contract, and overlay layouts or implementation. Fail if a remembered control disappears unexpectedly, labels overlap essential capture content, or a slider provides no usable value feedback. Static review cannot verify light-press/double-press/sliding ergonomics or lock-screen launch; list actual supported-device checks separately.

Use [SF Symbols](../../../apple-hig-foundations/.topics/apple-hig-sf-symbols/SKILL.md) for available symbol configuration and [Layout](../../../apple-hig-foundations/.topics/apple-hig-layout/SKILL.md) for adaptive overlay space.

# Camera Control Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/camera-control) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. The source describes Camera Control on iPhone 16 and 16 Pro. A light press opens a bezel-adjacent overlay, a light double press reveals controls, and sliding adjusts the selected control. ## Anatomy Use sliders for a continuous/value range and pickers for discrete choices. System zoom and exposure controls can accompany custom controls in the overlay. ## Best practices - Represent each function with an available SF Symbol; custom symbols are unsupported and the symbol represents function rather than live state. - Keep names short because Dynamic Type can enlarge labels over the viewfinder. Include units such as EV/% or a useful localized value string for sliders, and declare frequently used or regularly spaced prominent values for easier settling. - Leave overlay/label space next to the hardware control in portrait and landscape. Maximize the viewfinder, allowing the overlay over it, and hide duplicate app controls while the overlay is present. - Enable/disable the fixed set of controls according to capture mode; controls cannot be added/removed at runtime. - Put common controls near the middle and rare ones at either end. The system remembers the last control when reopening. - Provide a locked camera capture extension so people can launch the camera experience from lock screen, Home Screen, and other apps. ## Platform considerations The source marks Camera Control unsupported outside iOS. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/camera-control) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. ## Change log Source revision dates: September 9, 2024.

name: apple-hig-layout
description: Use when designing, reviewing, or adapting layout hierarchy, safe areas, size classes, resizable windows, enlarged text, or platform-specific spacing.
---

# Preserve relationships while available space changes

Read [Layout](../../references/layout.md). Inspect content priority, navigation, controls, supported environments, constraints, and current implementation. Identify design/review/adaptation mode and keep the existing layout system. Record actual available space and text/localization conditions; device names alone are insufficient evidence for a breakpoint.

Start with relationships: align peers, group related items, indent subordinates, and reveal secondary choices progressively. Place important content toward the leading/top region in the locale's reading order. Separate backgrounds that can extend beneath bars from important content/actions that must respect safe regions.

Choose adaptations from available width/height and environmental values, not a phone/tablet or portrait/landscape guess. Preserve selection, content, functionality, and idiom when columns collapse, actions overflow, or horizontal rows stack for larger text. Test the smallest and largest useful layouts first, then intermediate resizing, longer localization, direction changes, and display accommodations. Crop decorative backgrounds without distorting aspect ratio or hiding essential imagery.

Apply platform conditions deliberately: Mac essential controls cannot depend on a bottom edge that may be offscreen; TV content needs the guide's overscan insets and focus-expansion room; Watch normally needs very few side-by-side actions. visionOS windows/volumes should resize, use meaningful bounds, and avoid inline 3D crowding controls; use separate volumes for model-centric work. Read numeric platform specifications from the guide rather than generalizing one platform's spacing.

**Before → decision → after:** A reading list positions Delete at a fixed bottom coordinate and fixes each row to one line. Decision: resized windows and enlarged titles need flow-based layout. After, row height/wrapping adapt, secondary actions remain reachable through contextual overflow, and the selected article persists when the sidebar collapses.

Deliver corrected layouts/constraints or implementation plus an environment matrix. Fail if a required action disappears, related items detach, content overlaps hardware/bars, or resizing changes the task's meaning. Report tested dimensions/settings; static or Linux checks cannot establish native safe-area/focus behavior absent supported execution.

Use [Typography](../apple-hig-typography/SKILL.md) for text behavior, [Right to left](../apple-hig-right-to-left/SKILL.md) for direction, and [Spatial layout](../apple-hig-spatial-layout/SKILL.md) for 3D position/scale.

# Layout Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. Use predictable relationships among content and controls while adapting to the actual available space. ## Visual hierarchy Prioritize important content toward the top and leading edge in reading order. Use system components for RTL adaptation. Align related items, indent subordinate items, and group relationships with space, containers, or separators. Reveal secondary choices progressively through disclosure, menus, nested views, or scrollable media sections. Distinguish navigation/controls with Liquid Glass and scroll-edge treatments; extend full-window backgrounds under bars and sidebars. A background extension effect can mirror and blur imagery under adjacent components instead of hiding essential original art. ## Adaptability Handle size classes, display sizes, orientation/aspect ratio, Dynamic Island, external displays, Display Zoom, resizable windows, text changes, localized length/direction/fonts, and date/number formats. Use SwiftUI or Auto Layout, safe areas, margins, and layout modifiers. Orientation-locked games must still resize. With large text, stack horizontal content, increase row height, and allow wrapping. Apple’s Unity accessibility plug-in can supply Dynamic Type in games. Preview smallest/largest layouts first, then multiple devices, localizations, sizes, iPad resizing, and iPhone Mirroring. Scale backgrounds to fill without distorting aspect ratio; extreme wide/short or narrow/tall windows may crop much more than standard displays. ### Size classes Each axis is compact or regular, describing available width or height rather than device type or orientation. All four combinations can occur as apps resize, multitask, or mirror. Base layout on these environmental values, not idiom/orientation guesses. Preserve functionality across classes while changing how much is exposed, such as sidebar versus tabs or visible actions versus overflow. The platform idiom remains the same during resizing, so preserve its familiar character. ## Guides and safe areas Layout guides supply rectangular regions for alignment, spacing, margins, and readable text widths; custom guides can add app-specific structure. Safe areas exclude edge obstructions such as camera hardware, status bars, tab bars, and toolbars. Keep important content and controls within the appropriate safe regions. ## Platform considerations No extra iOS/iPadOS rules are listed. ### macOS Do not rely on the bottom of a window for essential controls because it may sit below the physical display. Avoid placing content behind the top camera housing. ### tvOS Inset primary content 60 pt vertically and 80 pt horizontally to withstand TV overscan/settings. Leave enough focus padding for system enlargement so focused items do not obscure important information. #### Grids Use consistent row/column spacing, sufficient room for enlargement, and symmetrical partial items at both horizontal edges. Add extra separation above and below row titles. UIKit collection flow layout derives the column count from item width and spacing. Source grid measurements follow; all use 40 pt horizontal gaps and a minimum 100 pt vertical gap between unfocused rows. #### Two-column grid Unfocused item width: 860 pt. Horizontal gap: 40 pt. Minimum vertical gap: 100 pt. #### Three-column grid Unfocused item width: 560 pt. Horizontal gap: 40 pt. Minimum vertical gap: 100 pt. #### Four-column grid Unfocused item width: 410 pt. Horizontal gap: 40 pt. Minimum vertical gap: 100 pt. #### Five-column grid Unfocused item width: 320 pt. Horizontal gap: 40 pt. Minimum vertical gap: 100 pt. #### Six-column grid Unfocused item width: 260 pt. Horizontal gap: 40 pt. Minimum vertical gap: 100 pt. #### Seven-column grid Unfocused item width: 217 pt. Horizontal gap: 40 pt. Minimum vertical gap: 100 pt. #### Eight-column grid Unfocused item width: 184 pt. Horizontal gap: 40 pt. Minimum vertical gap: 100 pt. #### Nine-column grid Unfocused item width: 160 pt. Horizontal gap: 40 pt. Minimum vertical gap: 100 pt. ### visionOS Support resizing in windows and volumes; center content horizontally at very large sizes. Set minimum/maximum bounds only to avoid overlaps or unwieldy layouts, not to disable resizing. Use inline 3D content sparingly for meaningful additions; inset it so it avoids controls and window edges. Prefer volumes or immersive spaces for large/model-centric content. Open supplemental content in an adjacent window, reserving ornaments for interactive app controls. Space controls so hover feedback remains distinct; regular buttons should have centers at least 60 pt apart. ### watchOS Normally use no more than three glyph buttons or two text buttons side by side. Full-width text controls usually work best; two short labels can fit on a non-scrolling screen. Support autorotation when people may show content, such as a photo or QR code, to another person or reader instead of always sleeping on wrist-away movement. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here. ## Change log Source revision dates: September 9, 2026, September 9, 2025, June 9, 2025, March 7, 2025, September 9, 2024, June 10, 2024, February 2, 2024, December 5, 2023, September 15, 2023, June 21, 2023, September 14, 2022.

description: Use when selecting or configuring SF Symbols, rendering modes, weights, variants, variable color, animations, custom symbols, or symbol availability.

# Configure the symbol's meaning before its decoration

Read [SF Symbols](../../references/sf-symbols.md). Inspect the intended action/state, neighboring type, background, deployment OS, and existing glyph implementation. Establish design, review, or adaptation mode. Produce the requested symbol assignment/configuration or custom-symbol specification within the existing stack. Check individual symbol/feature availability and licensing; library symbols cannot become product trademarks or app icons.

Select the semantic variant before styling: outline for ordinary text-adjacent controls, fill for supported emphasis/selection, enclosure for small-size clarity, or slash for negation. Let standard views choose variants when appropriate. Match symbol weight to adjacent text, then use scale to adjust emphasis without mismatching stroke weight.

Choose rendering by information. Monochrome suits one tint; hierarchical communicates layer importance; palette assigns intentional semantic colors; multicolor preserves intrinsic meaning. Variable color represents a quantity by activating layers and should exclude stable parts. It is not a substitute for hierarchy. Use adaptive colors and test the actual size/background rather than trusting automatic rendering.

If animating, select an effect whose meaning matches the event: a once-only bounce for feedback differs from ongoing pulse/breathe activity or a replacement state transition. Avoid simultaneous effects that conflict. For custom art, start from an appropriate template, preserve optical alignment, annotate whole layers/erase behavior and animation groups, and test presets. Do not modify restricted Apple product/feature symbols.

**Before → decision → after:** A fan control bounces forever and changes the whole icon's tint to show speed. Decision: rotation conveys operation while variable layers can convey quantity; the housing stays stable. After, an appropriate supported symbol configuration separates operating feedback from a labeled speed value, respects motion preferences, and keeps its housing readable.

Deliver names, supported variants/modes, state mapping, and fallback choices or implementation. Fail if a symbol is unavailable on the deployment OS, rendering erases a meaningful layer, or animation implies work after it stopped. Native/custom-symbol animation and localized variants require actual supported previews; static inspection cannot verify them.

Use [Icons](../apple-hig-icons/SKILL.md) when selecting a metaphor, [Motion](../apple-hig-motion/SKILL.md) for interaction timing, or [Right to left](../apple-hig-right-to-left/SKILL.md) for directional semantics.

# SF Symbols Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/sf-symbols) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. SF Symbols offers configurable glyphs aligned with San Francisco text. Check individual symbol and feature availability against the deployment OS. Symbols and confusingly similar forms must not become app icons, logos, or other trademarks; inspect the license and per-symbol restrictions. ## Rendering modes Symbols contain semantic layers. Monochrome gives all layers one tint with transparent cutouts. Hierarchical varies one tint’s opacity by layer importance. Palette assigns multiple colors; with two colors for three hierarchy levels, secondary and tertiary share a color. Multicolor uses intrinsic meaning-bearing colors and may allow tinting some layers. Use system colors for appearance/accessibility adaptation. Even automatic mode needs legibility checks at actual sizes and backgrounds. ## Gradients SF Symbols 7 adds single-source-color linear gradients across rendering modes, custom/system colors, and custom symbols. They work at all sizes but show best on large symbols. ## Variable color Represent changing strength, capacity, or another quantity by activating layers at thresholds from 0–100%. Exclude stable parts, such as a speaker body, from the changing layers. Use hierarchical rendering for depth; variable color communicates change rather than spatial hierarchy. ## Weights and scales Nine weights, ultralight through black, correspond to San Francisco text weights. Small, medium (default), and large scales are relative to cap height. Change scale to adjust symbol emphasis without breaking weight matching to same-point-size text. ## Design variants Outline generally suits text-adjacent lists/toolbars; fill adds emphasis for selected tabs and swipe actions. Enclosing circles/squares can improve small-size clarity; slash expresses negation/unavailability. Variants can combine, and standard views often select outline/fill automatically. Language/script variants adapt to device language across Latin, Arabic, Hebrew, Hindi, Thai, CJK, Cyrillic, Devanagari, and Indic numerals. ## Animations Use animations to convey an action, state, or ongoing work, with speed, repetition, reversal, and playback suited to that purpose and the app’s tone. Avoid concurrent effects that distract or send conflicting signals. |Effect|Meaning and behavior| |---|---| |Appear / Disappear|Gradual entry / exit| |Bounce|One elastic enlargement or movement then original state; normally plays once| |Scale|Persistent size change until reset or effect removal| |Pulse|Opacity changes on annotated layers or optionally all layers; useful for ongoing work| |Variable color|Cumulative or one-layer-at-a-time sequence; may autoreverse or hide inactive layers| |Replace|Down-up for state change, up-up for forward progression, off-up to emphasize next state| |Magic Replace|Related shapes intelligently transition badges/slashes; unrelated pairs fall back to down-up or a chosen direction| |Wiggle|Directional back-and-forth emphasis, including a potentially missed action| |Breathe|Opacity and size change together to suggest ongoing activity| |Rotate|Whole-symbol or selected-layer rotation, such as fan blades| |Draw On / Draw Off|SF Symbols 7 path drawing using guide points; simultaneous, staggered, or sequential layers| Variable-color open-loop symbols have endpoints that do not meet; closed-loop shapes support seamless continuous repetition. All library symbols and custom symbols can animate across modes, weights, and scales, but custom art needs testing. ## Custom symbols Export a similar template and edit vectors while matching detail, optical weight, alignment, position, and perspective. Keep the meaning simple, inclusive, recognizable, and directly tied to content or action. Do not modify copyrighted Apple product/feature symbols marked by an Info badge, nor reproduce those products in custom art. Annotate layers with hierarchy or colors for supported modes. Negative side margins can optically align wide badges; follow names such as `left-margin-Regular-M`. Annotate animation layers/groups and use Z-order for variable-color sequence direction. Test every preset. Whole underlying shapes plus an annotated erase layer preserve information for correct animation better than destructive cutouts. Use the component library for common badges/enclosures rather than baking variants into the base. Add accessible labels for custom symbols. ## Platform considerations No extra platform-specific rules are provided. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/sf-symbols) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here. ## Change log Source revision dates: July 28, 2025, June 10, 2024, June 5, 2023, September 14, 2022.

name: apple-hig-accessibility
description: Use when designing, reviewing, or adapting Apple-platform interfaces for text enlargement, sensory access, assistive input, motor access, cognitive needs, or accessibility preferences.

# Make the task accessible

Read [Accessibility guidance](../../references/accessibility.md) before applying platform values. This procedure turns that guidance into task-level changes; its artifact format and prioritization are application engineering advice, not additional Apple requirements.

## Establish what can be evaluated

Identify the supported platform, the person's task from entry to completion, and whether the request is design, review, or adaptation. Inspect the supplied screens, content, interaction description, semantics, or implementation. Record which evidence exists: a screenshot can establish visible labels and geometry, but cannot establish spoken names, focus order, alternative activation, or preference behavior. Continue using explicit assumptions when the platform or behavior is missing; ask only when the choice changes the requested result.

For a review, connect each finding to an observed barrier and its consequence for that task. Separate untested behavior needing verification from confirmed defects. For a design or adaptation, change the authorized artifact itself: a revised screen specification, interaction contract, or implementation. A general accessibility checklist alone is not the deliverable.

## Remove the barriers that the task contains

Trace the task without assuming sight, hearing, fine motor control, speech, or fast responses. Select the applicable branches:

- **Reading and visual distinctions:** Preserve content and available actions when text enlarges. Use the guide's platform-specific text defaults and minima; its resizing guidance is at least 200%, with 140% stated for watchOS. Reflow or expose another usable arrangement rather than clipping essential labels. Pair color distinctions with text, shape, or symbols. Evaluate actual foreground/background combinations in light and dark appearances; use a contrast calculator and preserve the guide's stated contrast-table scope instead of claiming that its values alone establish conformance. If the default scheme falls short, specify the Increase Contrast treatment.
- **Information carried by sound or imagery:** Identify what information would disappear when sound or sight is unavailable. Choose captions for synchronized audible events, subtitles for dialogue translation, audio description for visual events, or transcripts for a complete text account according to the content. Specify descriptions for meaningful interface/content imagery and omit redundant decoration. Pair essential sound feedback with a perceivable visual or appropriate haptic equivalent.
- **Manipulation and navigation:** Distinguish visible control size from its actual activation area and separation. Use the guide's platform default as the starting point; its smaller minimum is not a blanket recommendation for dense controls. Replace essential complex or repeated gestures with a labeled onscreen action. Make the complete task navigable and activatable with the supported keyboard and assistive input paths; speech must not be necessary. Preserve system accessibility shortcuts. For custom controls, specify names, roles, values, states, and task order rather than assuming their appearance supplies semantics.
- **Time, motion, and comprehension:** Give people time to read and act; prefer explicit dismissal when transient content requires attention. If motion is present, define a Reduce Motion version that retains state and meaning while reducing automatic movement, bounce, zoom, or depth changes. If media autoplays, provide playback control and consider a global preference; honor Dim Flashing Lights where applicable. Keep the task's navigation and wording consistent rather than adding instructional clutter.

Apply the relevant platform condition. For Assistive Access on iOS/iPadOS, focus on core tasks with one interaction per screen and the source's two confirmations for difficult-to-reverse actions in that mode. For visionOS, keep controls in comfortable view, avoid head-locked content and repeated large gestures, and accommodate hand/head Pointer Control and Zoom. These conditions do not apply automatically to every platform.

## Deliver and check the result

Return the revised artifact or evidence-based review, including the barrier, the concrete change, and its acceptance check. State which platform/preferences were considered and which claims remain unverified. Prioritize blockers to completing the task over cosmetic refinements.

Exercise each selected alternative along the same entry-to-completion path. Fail the check if essential content or actions disappear at the specified text scale, information remains available through only one sense, a required gesture has no equivalent, focus cannot reach/activate a necessary control, or a requested motion accommodation removes meaning. Measure contrast and activation geometry when the evidence permits; report missing measurements rather than inventing them. Use Accessibility Inspector and relevant VoiceOver, Switch Control, Full Keyboard Access, AssistiveTouch, or Pointer Control tests on supported Apple environments. Static inspection or a Linux run cannot establish those runtime results, Apple-device comfort, or App Store Accessibility Nutrition Label eligibility.

## Worked transformation

**Before:** An iPad astronomy log marks observation quality only with green/red dots, announces saving with a chime, and exposes Delete only by a two-finger gesture.

**Decision:** Logging must remain understandable without color or sound and operable without that gesture. Retain compact rows while making status and actions explicit.

**After:** Each row reads “Clear” or “Clouded” alongside its symbol; saving exposes a persistent “Saved” state; a labeled row action opens Delete. The screen specification includes expanded-text reflow, semantic row status, and keyboard/assistive activation acceptance checks. These are proposed changes until the actual implementation passes those checks; the specification does not claim VoiceOver was tested.

## Continue only where needed

For detailed spoken structure and rotor navigation, use [VoiceOver](../../../apple-hig-technologies/.topics/apple-hig-voiceover/SKILL.md). For text reflow/type choices use [Typography](../apple-hig-typography/SKILL.md); for a motion accommodation use [Motion](../apple-hig-motion/SKILL.md). If spatial comfort dominates the task, use [Spatial layout](../apple-hig-spatial-layout/SKILL.md). Keep the task's accessibility acceptance checks when handing off.

# Accessibility Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. Build an interface people can understand, perceive through different senses, and adapt to their preferred methods. Treat accessibility as a design input and audit with Accessibility Inspector. Evaluate actual support before describing Accessibility Nutrition Labels on the App Store. ## Vision Support text enlargement of at least 200%; the source gives 140% for watchOS. Dynamic Type or equivalent custom resizing must preserve usability. Follow platform defaults/minima when choosing custom styles, and enlarge thin-weight custom fonts further when needed. |Platform|Default text|Minimum text| |---|---:|---:| |iOS, iPadOS|17 pt|11 pt| |macOS|13 pt|10 pt| |tvOS|29 pt|23 pt| |visionOS|17 pt|12 pt| |watchOS|16 pt|12 pt| Measure contrast using established calculators such as WCAG or APCA. Apple’s Accessibility Inspector table uses these WCAG-AA guidance values: text up to 17 pt, all weights, 4.5:1; 18 pt at all weights, 3:1; bold text at any size, 3:1. Preserve the table’s stated scope rather than assuming it replaces a separate conformance evaluation. If default colors fall short, Increase Contrast must supply a higher-contrast scheme. Test both light and dark. Prefer semantic system colors that adapt to accessibility preferences. Pair color with shape, icons, or text; red/green and blue/orange distinctions can be difficult. Let people customize chart or character colors where useful. Give VoiceOver meaningful descriptions of interface and content. ## Hearing Make dialogue and important information available without sound. Captions describe audible information in synchrony with media, subtitles present dialogue in a chosen language, audio descriptions narrate otherwise visual events in audio pauses, and transcripts provide a complete text account of audible and visual information. Let people adjust text presentation. Pair sound feedback with matching haptics and visual direction cues, especially for offscreen game or spatial events. Music Haptics and audio graphs on iOS/iPadOS can offer tactile representations of music and data. ## Mobility Use comfortable controls and sufficient separation, not just adequate visible size. |Platform|Default control|Minimum control| |---|---:|---:| |iOS, iPadOS|44 × 44 pt|28 × 28 pt| |macOS|28 × 28 pt|20 × 20 pt| |tvOS|66 × 66 pt|56 × 56 pt| |visionOS|60 × 60 pt|28 × 28 pt| |watchOS|44 × 44 pt|28 × 28 pt| The source suggests around 12 pt padding for bezelled elements and 24 pt outside visible edges for elements without a bezel. Use simple gestures for repeated tasks and offer an onscreen alternative for essential gestures, such as a dismiss button alongside swipe-to-dismiss. Avoid requiring complex multiple-finger or multiple-hand actions. Label controls so Voice Control can target them. Siri/Shortcuts can expose repeated tasks through voice, Action buttons, Home Screen, and Control Center. Test VoiceOver, AssistiveTouch, Full Keyboard Access, Pointer Control, and Switch Control rather than assuming support. ## Speech Support complete keyboard navigation and Full Keyboard Access; preserve system accessibility shortcuts. Support Switch Control navigation and activation through hardware, controller, and sound inputs such as a click or pop, so speech is never a necessary input method. ## Cognitive Use familiar, simple, consistent navigation and gestures. Prefer explicit dismissal over timed disappearance, allowing time for processing and assistive navigation. Games can offer difficulty, reaction-time, success-criteria, and control-assistance accommodations. Give clear playback controls and consider a global autoplay preference. Respect Dim Flashing Lights during media playback. Honor Reduce Motion by reducing automatic and repeated movement, scaling, zooming, and peripheral effects. Reduce spring bounce; tie appropriate motion directly to gestures; avoid animated depth changes and blur transitions; replace spatial translations with fades. Fast or blinking motion can distract, cause dizziness, or trigger seizures. For Assistive Access on iOS/iPadOS, focus on core tasks, remove nonessential workflows, and split multistep tasks into one interaction per screen. The source requires two confirmations for actions that are difficult to reverse, such as deletion, in this mode. ## Platform considerations The source adds no separate rules for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, or watchOS beyond the guidance above. ### visionOS Support hand/head Pointer Control and Zoom. Keep controls inside a comfortable field of view; horizontal arrangements usually strain the neck less than tall ones. Avoid rapid shifts of attention among distant locations. Reduce peripheral animation speed and intensity, use gentle camera/video motion, and avoid making the surrounding world move without the person’s control. Do not lock content to the head, which can feel confining and interfere with Pointer Control. Minimize large or repeated gestures and consider the physical surroundings. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here. ## Change log Source revision dates: June 9, 2025, March 7, 2025, June 10, 2024, December 5, 2023, June 21, 2023.
